Experiments that changed questions

The mirror test: who recognises themselves?

A mark on the forehead and a mirror: chimpanzees touched the mark; monkeys did not. Babies manage it at about 18 months.

In 1970, the psychologist Gordon Gallup let some chimpanzees get used to a mirror. Then, while they were anaesthetised, he painted an odourless red mark on their foreheads. On waking and looking in the mirror, they touched the mark. Monkeys of other species, by contrast, kept treating their reflection as another animal.

Babies and other animals

A similar version is used with children, with a smudge of lipstick on the nose. At around 18 to 24 months, most touch their own nose when they look, instead of touching the mirror. It is a sign that they are starting to recognise themselves.

Orangutans, elephants, dolphins, magpies and, more controversially, a small fish, the cleaner wrasse, in 2019, have passed the test. The fish case revived the debate: does the test measure self-awareness or something simpler? It also favours animals that rely heavily on sight.

References

  1. Gallup, G. G. (1970). Chimpanzees: self-recognition. Science, 167(3914), 86–87.
  2. Kohda, M. et al. (2019). If a fish can pass the mark test, what are the implications for consciousness and self-awareness testing in animals? PLoS Biology, 17(2), e3000021.
